## The one-line version

**Before you signal a pid you did not launch, filter it through the session floor:**

```bash
scripts/session-floor.sh check <pid>          # exit 1 = protected, never signal
scripts/session-floor.sh filter $CANDIDATES   # safe pids on stdout, refusals on stderr
```

Better still, don't do pid math at all: `processes:kill { taskId }` kills the cgroup
subtree and cannot reach the session.

## What happened

On 2026-08-08 the owner was logged out of their desktop **twice**, by two different
agents, with two unrelated bugs — and one shared root cause: **no kill path on this
box had a floor protecting the owner's login session.**

### Trap 1 — the ancestor walk that stops at pid 1 (11:52:49 EDT)

An agent tearing down a Tauri test rig wanted to kill its app and the shell tree that
launched it:

```bash
CHAIN="$APP"; P=$(ps -o ppid= -p "$APP" | tr -d ' ')
# walk MY app's ancestor chain, stopping before systemd — exact pids only
while [ -n "$P" ] && [ "$P" != "1" ]; do CHAIN="$CHAIN $P"; P=$(ps -o ppid= -p "$P" | tr -d ' '); done
for p in $CHAIN; do kill "$p"; done
```

Read the comment: *"stopping before systemd"*. The author knew the hazard and believed
`1` was the systemd to stop before. But **`systemd --user` — the per-user session
manager — is an ordinary child of init, with PPID 1.** A walk that terminates when it
*reaches* 1 has already appended the user manager to `$CHAIN`.

And a user systemd manager treats **SIGTERM as "activate exit.target"** — which stops
every user service, tears down the graphical session, and logs the user out. The
journal showed `Activating special unit exit.target` two seconds after the command,
then `Session 2829 logged out` three seconds after that.

This is not an exotic mistake, and it is **easier to hit than it looks**: a backgrounded
agent job reparents to `systemd --user` once its launching shell exits, so an ancestor
walk starting from one reaches the user manager in a **single hop**.

A `PreToolUse` guard in `pretooluse-bash-resource-gate.sh` now denies the shape
(parent-walk **+** stop-at-1 **+** signal, all three required, so ordinary teardown and
read-only walks are untouched).

### Trap 2 — an unvalidated `grep -F` needle (20:32:15 EDT)

`fed_cleanup_scoped` in `papercusp-desktop/bin/lib/federation-asserts.sh` killed a run's
leftovers with:

```bash
ps -eo pid,args | grep -F "$work" | grep -v grep | awk '{print $1}' | while read -r pid; do
  kill -9 "$pid"
done
```

A fuzz harness enumerated every `fed_*` function with `declare -F` and called each with
placeholder args `a b c d 1 e f`. So `$work` arrived as **`"a"`**, and `grep -F a`
matched nearly every process on the box: **1,896 SIGKILLs in one second**, including
`gnome-session-binary`. The user manager survived only by luck —
`/usr/lib/systemd/systemd --user` happens to contain no letter `a`.

The validation *existed* (`fed_is_rig_work`) but guarded `fed_cleanup_run`, the **public
door**, while the function that actually signals trusted its caller. **A guard on a door
is not a guard on the thing behind it — validate at the point of danger.**

## The 15-char comm trap (this one nearly shipped in the fix itself)

The first version of the session floor used `pgrep -x gnome-session-binary`. It matched
**zero rows**:

```
pgrep: pattern that searches for process name longer than 15 characters
       will result in zero matches
```

The kernel clips `/proc/<pid>/comm` to 15 chars (`TASK_COMM_LEN` 16, incl. NUL), so
`gnome-session-binary` is really `gnome-session-b`. pgrep prints a warning to stderr and
still **exits cleanly** — so the floor cheerfully reported *"safe to kill"* for the exact
process whose death ended the owner's session, and nothing in its output looked wrong.

Three of the obvious names truncate: `gnome-session-binary` → `gnome-session-b`,
`gdm-wayland-session` → `gdm-wayland-ses`, `gnome-session-ctl` → `gnome-session-c`.
**Always truncate a comm name to 15 chars before comparing.**

Related: use `pgrep -x` (exact comm) and never `pgrep -f` for this — `-f` reads the full
command line, so it matches any peer agent's shell that merely *mentions* the name,
including your own probe. See
[exit-144-pkill-self-match](/internal/docs/agent-insights/exit-144-pkill-self-match).

## What the floor protects

`scripts/lib/session-floor.sh` refuses: pid 1 · `systemd --user` · every seat-attached
logind session **Leader** · `gnome-session-b` · `gnome-shell` · `gnome-session-c` ·
`Xorg` / `Xwayland` · `gdm-x-session` / `gdm-wayland-ses` / `gdm` (plus KDE equivalents).
It fails **closed**: garbage or unreadable input is treated as protected.

## Transferable rules

1. **A parent walk's stop condition should be the session boundary, not pid 1.** If you
   are walking ancestors to kill them, you are one layer away from the user manager.
2. **Validate at the kill site, not at the public door.** Any other caller — a selftest,
   a fuzzer, a future rig, a human sourcing the file — reaches the dangerous line directly.
3. **Cap the blast radius independently of the validation.** "One run's leftovers" is
   never 1,600 processes. A cap needs no notion of what a valid input looks like, so it
   still holds when the validator's assumptions go stale.
4. **Key a guard on the DANGER, not on a convenient list.** Guarding by the hardcoded
   `/tmp/<rig>.` prefix list would have broken a live rig that legitimately uses
   `$HOME/.papercusp-lane-a-fed`, while *still* not describing the hazard. The hazard was
   non-specificity; that is what the guard measures.
5. **An empty forensics log means "this instrument cannot see that mechanism", not
   "nothing happened".** A D-Bus monitor installed for this exact class (WI-4674) recorded
   nothing, because it watched `StartUnit` method calls and the real mechanism was a
   *signal*. Its clean gap across the incident reads exactly like innocence.

Related: [desktop-session-liveness-ancestry](/internal/docs/agent-insights/desktop-session-liveness-ancestry)
(the sibling problem — detecting an on-desktop session so a reaper *exempts* it).
